title: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — BIBLICAL WAITING IS NOT DOING NOTHING
paragraphs: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — BIBLICAL WAITING IS NOT DOING NOTHING
You thought God was making you wait because nothing was happening. But what if the waiting room is actually the workshop where God is rebuilding the person who will walk through the next door?
There is a kind of exhaustion sleep cannot fix.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up tired.
You can take a vacation and still feel something inside you dragging its feet.

You can smile at church, answer “I’m blessed” when somebody asks how you are doing, post a Scripture verse, encourage somebody else, and then sit alone later wondering why God seems so painfully quiet about the one thing you have begged Him to change.
At least, nothing you can see.
The child has not come home.
The financial pressure has not disappeared.
The temptation has not stopped knocking.
The answer you thought would arrive in weeks has taken months.
And somewhere between “Lord, I trust You” and “Lord, how much longer?” you became tired.
That is exactly where one of Scripture’s most beloved promises becomes far more powerful than the inspirational sentence we sometimes make it.
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.”
Because there is something hiding inside that word wait.
The opening expression, וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה — veqovey YHWH, speaks of those who wait for, hope in, or look expectantly toward the LORD.
The Hebrew verb behind it is קָוָה — qavah.
It carries the biblical idea of waiting with hope and expectation.
Biblical waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is not sitting on the floor saying, “Well, I guess God will do everything.”
It is not procrastination dressed in Christian vocabulary.
Waiting on God is a posture of dependent expectation.
You continue trusting when you cannot yet see.
You continue obeying when obedience has not yet produced the outcome you wanted.
You continue praying when heaven feels quiet.
You continue walking when your emotions are begging you to quit.
You keep your eyes on the character of God when circumstances seem to contradict the promises of God.
And sometimes waiting requires more faith than moving.
Because movement can make us feel powerful.
Waiting reminds us that we are not.
Maybe that is why you hate it.
Maybe that is why I hate it.
When there is something we can fix, we can become the hero.
When there is somebody we can call, a strategy we can execute, money we can spend, a door we can force open, or a problem we can solve, we can maintain the illusion that we are in control.
But eventually life brings you somewhere your hands cannot reach.
A prayer without an immediate answer.
A season where every plan collapses.
And suddenly your résumé cannot rescue you.
Your religious vocabulary cannot rescue you.
You discover something terrifying and liberating at the same time:
And perhaps one of the hidden mercies of waiting is that it slowly kills the illusion that you ever were.
Isaiah 40 was not originally written as a decorative slogan for comfortable people having a difficult Monday.
Its message addresses people confronted with weakness, discouragement, and the overwhelming greatness of God.
Just before the famous promise, Isaiah asks:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?”
God has not misplaced His people.
God has not reached the end of His wisdom.
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?”
Read that again when you are exhausted.
You become weary. God does not.
You lose perspective. God does not.
You become confused. God does not.
You see today. God sees what you cannot.
You reach the edge of your strength.
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.”
The people who have finally stopped pretending they have an unlimited supply.
And then Scripture goes even further:
“Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall.”
In other words, even natural strength eventually fails.
Human strength has an expiration date.
You do not know what tomorrow holds.
“They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength.”
And the Hebrew expression becomes even more fascinating here:
The verb חָלַף — chalaph can carry the sense of changing, passing on, or renewing.
In Isaiah 40:31, the idea is that those hoping in the LORD receive renewed strength.
Do not turn that into a mystical formula.
Isaiah is not promising that believers become physically invincible.
He is revealing the sufficiency of God for people who have reached the end of themselves.
And perhaps the breakthrough you desperately need is not always God immediately changing your circumstances.
Sometimes it is God sustaining and changing you in the middle of them.
That may not be the miracle you requested.
But do not underestimate that miracle.
Because there are prayers God answers by removing the mountain.
And there are seasons in which God teaches His people to walk faithfully while the mountain is still standing.
He pleaded with the Lord concerning his “thorn in the flesh.”
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
Christian faith does not teach that every painful circumstance disappears if you pray hard enough.
Sometimes God delivers from the fire.
Sometimes faithful believers die while still trusting God.
Read Hebrews 11 all the way to the end.
Biblical faith is not confidence that God must write the chapter exactly the way we demand.
Biblical faith is confidence that God remains faithful even when we cannot understand the chapter He has permitted us to enter.
And that is where waiting becomes worship.
“Jesus, I still trust You when I cannot trace You.”
“I will not manufacture an Ishmael because I am impatient for Isaac.”
Abraham and Sarah knew what happens when human beings become tired of waiting.
Then human ingenuity entered the story.
Genesis 16 records the painful consequences surrounding Hagar and Ishmael after Abraham and Sarah attempted to solve through human arrangement what God had promised according to His own purpose.
How often do we do the same thing?
We start looking for a window to crawl through.
And then we ask God to bless the thing our impatience created.
Some of the deepest scars in our lives did not come because God abandoned us.
They came because we became terrified that His timing could not be trusted.
But grace is not afraid to expose what it intends to heal.
Maybe you are waiting right now.
Waiting for someone to love you.
And loneliness is whispering, “Take whoever will stay, even if they pull you away from Christ.”
Maybe you are waiting for financial relief.
And desperation is whispering, “Compromise just this once.”
Maybe you are waiting for recognition.
And insecurity is whispering, “Promote yourself. Exaggerate. Make people notice.”
Maybe you are waiting for justice.
And anger is whispering, “Destroy them before God deals with it.”
Maybe you are waiting for restoration.
And shame is whispering, “God is finished with you.”
Because if you belong to Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
One night he was certain he was strong enough.
Imagine the silence after the rooster crowed.
Imagine realizing that the Jesus you swore you would never abandon had heard your denial.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
The kind of moment you wish could be deleted from Scripture.
But Jesus did not delete Peter.
After the resurrection, John 21 gives us one of the most tender restoration scenes in the Bible.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally learned how to become strong enough.
It is the announcement that sinners who could never save themselves have been offered mercy through the crucified and risen Son of God.
Jesus did not wait for us to repair ourselves.
He bore sin at the cross.
And forgiveness is not purchased by our religious performance.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can rescue you.
Maybe the waiting season is exposing something in you right now.
But because whatever grace exposes, we no longer have to keep pretending is not there.
Your fear that if God does not give you what you want, He cannot possibly love you.
Do not hide it behind church language.
The enemy wants your failure to become a hiding place.
Jesus calls sinners into the light.
And maybe somebody reading this has been hiding for a very long time.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You have been performing Christianity instead of abiding in Christ.
You have been carrying everyone else while secretly wondering who would carry you.
You have been telling people God is faithful while crying at night because you are struggling to believe those same words for yourself.
Not merely to the person who has everything together.
There is no shame in admitting:
That confession may become the place where dependence begins.
Waiting on the Lord does not mean you stop doing what God has already told you to do.
Seek wise counsel while you wait.
Love your family while you wait.
Take the next faithful step while you wait.
If there is sin to abandon, abandon it.
If there is an apology to make, make it.
If there is work God has placed before you, do it faithfully.
If there is medical, pastoral, financial, or professional help you genuinely need, seeking appropriate help is not necessarily a failure to trust God.
Waiting on the Lord is not refusing every available means while demanding a miracle.
It is refusing to make an idol of the means.
You work, but God is your hope.
You seek counsel, but God is your hope.
You plan, but God is your hope.
You receive treatment, but God is your hope.
You knock on doors, but God is your hope.
You do what faithfulness requires without pretending that your own hands are sovereign.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”
“They shall run, and not be weary.”
Unless you have lived long enough to understand that sometimes walking is the miracle.
You feel the wind beneath your faith.
But then there are seasons when getting out of bed and still saying “Jesus, I trust You” is an act of warfare.
You prayed even though you cried through half the prayer.
You opened your Bible even though your mind wandered.
You went to church even though you felt numb.
You resisted the temptation one more night.
You did not send the message you knew you should not send.
You chose truth over the lie.
You refused to abandon Christ because your circumstances hurt.
Some victories do not sound like thunder.
Sometimes victory sounds like exhausted footsteps still moving toward Jesus.
That is why waiting is not doing nothing.
Waiting is where roots grow beneath ground nobody applauds.
He received dreams, but the palace did not arrive the next morning.
Genesis even records that the chief cupbearer forgot Joseph for a time.
And when the appointed circumstances converged, Joseph was brought before Pharaoh.
Years that might have looked wasted became part of the road God used in preserving many lives.
That does not make betrayal good.
It means evil does not outrank God's sovereignty.
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
Notice Scripture does not call their evil good.
That is hope for somebody carrying scars.
What happened to you may genuinely have been wrong.
Christian faith does not require you to rename darkness as light.
It tells you that darkness does not get the final word over those held by God.
The innocent Christ hanging between criminals.
To the disciples, Friday looked like catastrophe.
But Saturday was not the ending.
And suddenly the darkest chapter became the doorway into the proclamation that would echo across nations:
This is why Christians can wait without worshiping despair.
Our hope is ultimately not that every earthly story will become comfortable.
So perhaps you are living in a Saturday season.
And you cannot yet see resurrection on the horizon.
Do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Do not confuse delay with abandonment.
Do not confuse waiting with inactivity.
And do not build your theology around one painful afternoon.
Maybe they take longer than you want.
Scripture does not give us permission to manufacture dates God has not revealed.
But it gives us something deeper than a deadline.
And if your strength is almost gone, maybe your prayer tonight does not need to sound impressive.
So give me grace to obey You today.
Heal what You desire to heal.
Close the doors I keep trying to force open.
Give me courage to walk through the doors You open.
And surrender to Christ is not the end of your story.
It may be where the rewriting begins.
There may be another believer reading the comments who knows exactly what that kind of night feels like.

And if God has already carried you through a long waiting season, tell somebody what He taught you. Your testimony may become encouragement for the person who is currently standing where you once stood.
Not because every sentence will solve tomorrow.
The mother still praying for her child.
The husband fighting for his marriage.
The widow learning to wake up alone.
The believer fighting a secret temptation.
The person waiting on medical answers.
The Christian who is beginning to wonder whether God still sees them.
Do not assume they already know you care.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you return to Scripture, pointing you toward repentance, reminding you of grace, and keeping Jesus Christ in front of you when the noise of the world keeps pulling your eyes elsewhere, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.
Following Gospel Warrior costs nothing, and sharing these messages costs nothing. Both genuinely help the message travel farther.
It does not purchase answered prayer.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
So support should never be manipulated out of fear or spiritual pressure.
Creating biblical resources takes time and resources.
Reaching another person who has never understood grace matters.
Helping someone open Scripture again matters.
Helping someone encounter the Gospel matters.
But the merchandise is not the mission.
And the deeper reason to stay connected is spiritual nourishment.
Invite the Christian who has drifted.
Invite the person who is skeptical.
Invite the person who has been wounded by religion and needs to see the difference between human hypocrisy and Jesus Christ.
Invite the person who needs Scripture more than another motivational slogan.
Because perhaps the next article they encounter will reach them on the night they were considering giving up.
Perhaps one verse will send them back to the Bible.
Perhaps one testimony will make them pray again.
Perhaps one Gospel message will remind them that grace is still calling.
We can refuse to keep good news to ourselves.
And maybe that is part of what God is teaching you in the waiting.
You thought waiting meant your life was on pause.
But God was teaching you dependence.
You thought your weakness disqualified you.
Christ was teaching you where real strength comes from.
You thought the closed door meant rejection.
You thought the silence meant absence.
God had not moved from His throne.
You thought you needed an explanation.
God was inviting you to trust His character.
You thought you needed enough strength for the next ten years.
God was giving you enough grace for the next step.
When everybody else seems to be passing you…
When you have to repent again…
When shame tells you to hide…
When you do not understand what God is doing…
keep your eyes on who God has revealed Himself to be.
Because the promise was never that those who wait upon the Lord would never become tired.
The promise is that exhausted human beings do not have to make their own strength their final hope.
Those who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength.
Maybe you entered this season asking God:
And perhaps one of the questions worth asking now is:
“Jesus, who are You forming me to become while I am here?”
And when strength returns, remember where it came from.
But because grace, when it captures a heart, teaches us to stop living only for ourselves.
And remember this when the night feels longest:
The waiting room may feel silent, but the Author has not put down the pen.
